d_sv_content.name: Pilot clinical trial of anti-cancer therapy with trametinib in naturally occurring acute myeloid leukemia
d_sv_content.tagline: Help investigate new ways to battle acute myeloid leukemia!
d_sv_content.description:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a fast-growing cancer of the blood and bone marrow that affects both people and dogs. Dogs diagnosed with AML usually have a poor outlook, and current treatments only extend survival for a short time, typically about 1–2 months.

Researchers are looking for better treatment options for dogs with AML. Many dogs with AML have changes (mutations) in a gene called NRAS, which can cause cancer cells to grow and survive. This study is testing a medication called trametinib, which blocks signals that cancer cells use to grow.

The purpose of this study is to find out whether trametinib is safe for dogs with AML and whether it may help slow down or reduce the cancer. Information learned from this study may also help researchers better understand leukemia in people.

This trial is being led by the Clinical Hematopathology Laboratory in partnership with the Flint Animal Cancer Center of the Colorado State University Veterinary Health System and is sponsored by the Lutsen Linder Research Fund for Extremely Gorgeous Dogs.
d_sv_content.requirements: All study visits are done with the pet's local oncologist; travel to Colorado State University is not required.Enrollment VisitPhysical examination and review of medical records.Blood collection for testing.Urine sample collection.Cheek swab (buccal swab) for DNA banking and future genetic research.Start of prednisone treatmentStart of trametinib treatment at homeTreatmentDaily trametinib medication given by mouth at homeDaily prednisone and any additional supportive medications prescribed by the veterinarianFollow-Up VisitsVisits at Weeks 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, and 12, then every 4 weeks after that while your dog remains in the study.Physical examinations and health updatesBlood tests to monitor your dog's health and response to treatmentUrine testing every 4 weeks (or more often if needed)Samples CollectedBlood samples for routine testing and leukemia monitoringUrine samplesOne cheek swab collected at enrollmentNo bone marrow biopsies are required for this studyLength of ParticipationYour dog can stay in the study as long as:The treatment is toleratedThe leukemia remains stable or improvesParticipation will end if:The disease worsensSide effects become unacceptableThe owner chooses to withdrawThe study veterinarian determines removal is necessaryThe dog dies or is euthanized
d_sv_content.responsibilities: Sign the informed consent form before enrollment.Give trametinib and prednisone exactly as directed.Keep a log of trametinib administration and any side effects your dog hasBring your dog to all scheduled study visits.Fill out an online survey at each study visit to provide information about your dog's health, behavior, and any side effects.Inform the study team of any concerns or changes in your dog's condition.Follow study instructions and treatment recommendations throughout participation.
d_sv_content.whoCan: Dogs May Be Eligible If They:Have a confirmed diagnosis of acute myeloid leukemia (AML)Have leukemia cells present in their bloodstream so the disease can be monitored over timeComplete initial testing, including blood work and urinalysisRemain generally active and able to carry out normal activitiesHave an owner willing to follow study requirements and attend follow-up visitsDogs Cannot Participate If They:Are currently receiving other anti-cancer treatments or have not completed the required washout period from previous chemotherapy.Have severe health conditions (such as serious kidney, liver, or heart disease) that could interfere with treatment or study results.Are considered unsuitable for participation by the attending veterinarian.
d_sv_content.benefits: Possible BenefitsYour dog may experience clinical improvement or live longer than expected with currently available treatments.Your dog will receive close monitoring from veterinary specialists.The information gained may help develop better treatments for future dogs with AML.Findings from this research may also contribute to leukemia research in people.Possible RisksTrametinib may cause side effects, including:Tiredness or lethargyUpset stomach, vomiting, or diarrheaHigh blood pressureProtein in the urineChanges in bloodwork, including liver enzyme abnormalities or low blood protein levelsOther possible risks include:Temporary discomfort from blood draws and examinationsThe treatment may not help your dog's leukemiaUnexpected side effects may occurTo reduce these risks, dogs will receive regular examinations, laboratory testing, and medication adjustments if side effects develop.
d_sv_content.compensation: The study will cover the cost for study medication (trametinib and prednisone), study-related diagnostic monitoring, and sample shipping.
d_sv_content.timeCommitment: Visits are every two weeks up until week 12. Then, a visit every 4 weeks.
